title: Shelach: go and see (Numbers 13:1–2)
hookLine: twelve scouts are sent to see the land

lines: AT THE EDGE OF THE LAND.
cards: Before you sign a lease, you visit the apartment. You open the closets, run the shower, check whether the windows face a brick wall. Before a big move, people drive through the new town at night to see if it's quiet.
Nobody wants to commit to a place sight unseen. The Israelites are camped in the wilderness of Paran, at the edge of the promised land. The next step is to walk in.
And first, someone wants a look around.

teach.b: God says to Moses: "Send thou men, that they may spy out the land of Canaan". In Hebrew, shelach lecha: send for yourself. That extra word, lecha, caught Rashi's eye.
He reads it as permission, not command: send if you want to; I'm not ordering it. Why put it that way? Because in Deuteronomy, Moses remembers that the people asked for it.
So twelve men go, one leader from each tribe. One of them, Hoshea, gets a new name from Moses: Yehoshua, Joshua.

teach.h: MOSES' LIST: SEE WHAT IT IS.
teach.b: Moses gives them a careful list of questions. See the land, what it is. The people living there: strong or weak, few or many.
The cities: open camps or fortified. The soil: rich or poor. Are there trees?
Be of good courage, he says, and bring back some of its fruit. It was the season of the first ripe grapes. They go for forty days, from the south to the far north.
Past Hebron, in a valley later called Eshcol, cluster, they cut a single bunch of grapes so heavy that two men carry it between them on a pole.
Pomegranates and figs too. The verb for their mission, latur, means to scout, to explore, to go around and look. Looking isn't the problem.
Moses asked them to see, and to bring back something real. What they do with what they saw, as we'll find, is the test.

how: Shelach is read in synagogue in the yearly Torah cycle; the image of two scouts carrying a giant grape cluster on a pole is a familiar one in Jewish art, and the story of the scouts is studied as a lesson in how people see and report.

the grape cluster carried back on a pole
send: the portion of the twelve scouts

games.q: the scouts set out — tap the pairs.

s: Rashi reads "send for yourself" as permission, not a command
send if you want; the people had asked for it.
the scouts brought back a grape cluster carried by two men on a pole
from a valley they named Eshcol, cluster.
Moses sent the scouts with no instructions
he gave them a list: the land, the people, the cities, the soil, the trees, and the fruit.

games.q: you're Moses, sending scouts into the land. what do you ask them to bring back?
o: nothing; just a yes or no.
answers about the land and its people, and some of its fruit.
games.why: Moses asks them to see what it is, strong or weak, rich or poor, and to be of good courage and bring back fruit.

practice: Think of one thing you've formed an opinion about secondhand, a neighborhood, a coworker, a book you've only heard about, and notice where the opinion came from: a review, a rumor?
Then picture going to see for yourself, and ask Moses' first question: what is it, really?
